items.title: Al Rose Interview, 1975-02-19
items.q: I consider Johnny Wiggs to be the most competent musician I ever knew.

ctx.x: And, okay, what, let me just ask you this before we close, because we're getting close. Who have you closely worked with that you've particularly been impressed by?
Oh, Johnny Wiggs. I consider Johnny Wiggs to be the most competent musician I ever knew.
Nobody knows who Johnny Wiggs is.

items.title: Al Rose Interview, 1975-02-03
items.q: I think you were at Woodman of the World Hall when we made the Kingsville Parade with Johnny Wiggs and Raymond Burke and Emil Christian, Jeff Riddick, Paul Barberan, Sherwood Mangiapani.

ctx.x: Well, I don't want to mention names in this, but I've had the experience of, say, working with Johnny Wiggs or Percy Humphrey at concerts. It's getting really off the subject of you, but it's your perception of the music and what perspective. And you can change one person, get rid of Wiggs in a band, say, for example. And the whole band is changing the whole attitude.

Of course it is. It's because of the fact that a trumpet player like Johnny Wiggs knows the role of the cornet in the jazz band. He understands the nature of the lead. And most musicians are thinking in terms of each of his own performance, you see. And he does not know anymore how to listen to the sound of a band. And I get the feeling that he doesn't even really enjoy the sound of the band particularly, but is only considering what he himself is doing. And this is something that is relatively new in New Orleans…
I feel that there's a loss of respect for the music and the audience both.
